key_insight: STEM replaces the FFN up-projection with a static, token-indexed layer-local embedding lookup while keeping the gate and down-projection dense, removing runtime routing and enabling CPU offload with asynchronous prefetch to scale parameters without proportional per-token compute.
problem_solved: Addresses instability, load-balancing and communication overheads of fine-grained sparsity / MoE-style approaches, enabling higher parametric capacity without costly per-token routing or heavy inter-device communication.
method: Replace FFN up-projection with a layer-local token-indexed embedding lookup (static assignment — no runtime routing).
Keep the gate and down-projection dense to preserve expressivity and training stability.
Enable CPU offload of the embedding modules with asynchronous prefetch to decouple parameter capacity from per-token GPU compute and reduce communication overhead.
impact: Provides a practical path to much larger effective model capacity with lower per-token cost and fewer engineering/communication headaches — easier to scale and deploy while maintaining stable training and good throughput.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic of a Transformer FFN block: standard dense FFN vs STEM (embedding lookup replacing up-projection + dense gate/down-projection).
Pipeline diagram showing CPU offload + asynchronous prefetch feeding GPU compute (illustrating decoupling of capacity and per-token compute).
Performance chart comparing throughput, memory footprint, and perplexity (or accuracy) for Dense vs MoE vs STEM across increasing parameter counts.
Icon set highlighting key wins: 'No runtime routing', 'Lower communication', 'Stable training', 'Higher param capacity'.
paper_title: STEM: Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules
paper_authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Sheng Cao, Harry Dong, Changsheng Zhao, Attiano Purpura-Pontoniere
